params.body:
The `two_factor` flag stands at `admins`. The one thing between it and a rollout to every dealer is that there is no way back: a user who lost both his phone and his recovery codes cannot get in, and nobody could let him.

Shane, 21 September 2026, chose who may: Stocklist support, nobody else. That is not an arbitrary line. Through "inloggen als" (R P2-11.8) support already reaches that account, and delegation deliberately never asks for a second factor (R P2-3.19), so this adds no power to whoever holds it — it gives the user his own sign-in back. Putting it with the dealer would add power: whoever manages users could take a colleague's second factor away and then sign in as that colleague.

What goes: the secret, the recovery codes, the confirmation and the device secret, so every remembered-device cookie of that user dies too (R P2-3.16) and a stolen phone is left with nothing. Passkeys stay — they sit behind the fingerprint or PIN of their own device and are a second way in, not a second factor.

The owner of the account is told by mail, with who and when, in his own language. That is the safeguard rather than the courtesy: the account is enterable with a password alone again, and whoever did not ask for that has to hear it from us at that moment. A mail that fails does not hold up the recovery — the reason goes to the log and the user is on the phone waiting.

The button only shows for support and only on a user who actually has a second factor, and the action checks the right again itself rather than trusting the screen. The test proves that a dealer administrator gets a 403 and not merely a redirect from the menu rights.

New rule R P2-3.22.
params.title: Staff can reset a second factor
